did_you_know.text: Did you know? The king of Tyre is described as becoming so arrogant that he said, “I am a god,” and claimed divine status for himself, even though the prophecy emphasizes: “You are a man and not a god.”
Did you know? The wisdom of the king of Tyre is presented as exceptionally advanced human wisdom, but not divine wisdom. His confidence in his wisdom and wealth was one of the causes of his pride.
Did you know? The punishment for the king of Tyre’s pride is the arrival of “foreigners” and “the most ruthless of the nations,” who will destroy his power and profane his beauty.
Did you know? Alongside the prophecy against the ruler of Tyre, there is also a lament over the “king of Tyre,” portraying him as a figure of exceptional wisdom, beauty, and wealth.

Did you know? The lament uses images of Eden, precious stones, gold, and musical instruments to describe the splendor of the king of Tyre; the description does not necessarily have to be understood as a literal historical account.

Did you know? The king of Tyre is portrayed symbolically as a “cherub” dwelling on the holy mountain among the fiery stones. This image emphasizes his exalted status, but the rest of the chapter makes clear that he sinned and was expelled from his position.
Did you know? According to the lament, Tyre’s extensive trade became filled with violence, and the injustice in its activities led to its profanation and downfall.
Did you know? Pride in beauty and wealth corrupted the wisdom of the king of Tyre. In the prophecy, he is cast down to the ground and becomes a spectacle before the nations.
Did you know? After the prophecies against Tyre, Ezekiel is commanded to turn his attention to Sidon and prophesy judgment against it.
Did you know? The chapter ends with hope for Israel: the Lord will gather the house of Israel from among the nations, return it to its land, and sanctify his name before the nations.
